take-pregnancy-test.title: Take a home pregnancy test
take-pregnancy-test.detail: Most tests are reliable from the first day of a missed period. If it's negative but your period still doesn't come, test again a few days later.

start-folic-acid.title: Take folic acid every day
start-folic-acid.detail: 400 micrograms a day, ideally from before conception until 12 weeks. Your doctor may advise a higher dose in some situations.

review-medicines.title: Review your medicines and supplements
review-medicines.detail: Ask a doctor or pharmacist before starting or stopping anything, and avoid supplements containing vitamin A (retinol).

stop-alcohol-and-smoking.title: Stop alcohol and smoking
stop-alcohol-and-smoking.detail: No amount of alcohol is known to be safe in pregnancy. If you smoke, ask your doctor or midwife about support to quit.

limit-caffeine.title: Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day
limit-caffeine.detail: That's about two mugs of instant coffee. Tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate contain caffeine too.

learn-food-safety.title: Learn which foods to avoid
learn-food-safety.detail: Such as unpasteurised dairy, raw or undercooked meat, liver, and fish high in mercury like shark and swordfish.

book-first-appointment.title: Book your first pregnancy appointment
book-first-appointment.detail: Often called the booking appointment, it usually happens between 8 and 12 weeks and covers your health history, tests and care options.

ask-about-vitamin-d.title: Ask about vitamin D
ask-about-vitamin-d.detail: Many people are advised to take a daily vitamin D supplement in pregnancy. Recommended amounts vary by country.

first-blood-tests.title: Have your first blood tests
first-blood-tests.detail: These usually check your blood group and Rh (D) status, iron levels and infections such as HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis.

flu-and-covid-vaccines.title: Ask about flu and COVID-19 vaccines
flu-and-covid-vaccines.detail: The flu vaccine can be given at any stage of pregnancy during flu season. Ask whether a COVID-19 vaccine is advised for you.

decide-on-screening.title: Decide about screening tests
decide-on-screening.detail: You may be offered the combined test (about 10 to 14 weeks) or NIPT (from 10 weeks). Whether to have screening is your choice.

dating-scan.title: Have your dating scan
dating-scan.detail: Usually between 10 and 14 weeks, it checks your baby's development and confirms your due date.

dental-check-up.title: Book a dental check-up
dental-check-up.detail: Gum problems are common in pregnancy. Let your dentist know you're pregnant.

pelvic-floor-exercises.title: Start daily pelvic floor exercises
pelvic-floor-exercises.detail: Squeeze and lift the muscles you'd use to hold in pee, hold for a few seconds, then relax. They help prevent leaks now and after birth.

whooping-cough-vaccine.title: Ask about the whooping cough vaccine
whooping-cough-vaccine.detail: Usually given between 16 and 32 weeks in the UK or 27–36 weeks in the US. It helps protect your baby in the first weeks of life.

choose-birth-place.title: Think about where to give birth
choose-birth-place.detail: Options such as a hospital, birth centre or home birth vary by area. You can change your mind later.

maternity-leave-rights.title: Look into maternity leave and pay
maternity-leave-rights.detail: Rules and deadlines vary by country and employer. Note when you need to tell your employer and claim any pay.

anomaly-scan.title: Have your anomaly (anatomy) scan
anomaly-scan.detail: This detailed scan, usually between about 18 and 22 weeks, checks how your baby is growing and developing.

pregnancy-certificate.title: Get a pregnancy certificate for work
pregnancy-certificate.detail: Some employers and benefit schemes need a certificate from your doctor or midwife, such as the MAT B1 form in the UK.

pre-eclampsia-signs.title: Learn the warning signs of pre-eclampsia
pre-eclampsia-signs.detail: A severe headache, vision problems, pain just below the ribs or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet need urgent checking.

book-antenatal-classes.title: Book antenatal classes
book-antenatal-classes.detail: Classes on labour, birth and feeding can help you feel prepared. Popular ones fill up early.

glucose-test.title: Glucose test for gestational diabetes
glucose-test.detail: Often done between 24 and 28 weeks, either for everyone or if you have risk factors, depending on where you live.

know-baby-movements.title: Get to know your baby's movements
know-baby-movements.detail: There's no set number of kicks to count. If movements slow down, change or stop, call your maternity unit straight away.

partner-leave.title: Check leave for your partner
partner-leave.detail: If your partner plans time off around the birth, they may need to tell their employer by a set date.

baby-essentials-list.title: Make a list of baby essentials
baby-essentials-list.detail: Start with a safe place to sleep, a car seat, clothes, nappies and feeding supplies. Borrowed items are fine, but use a new mattress if you can.

anti-d-if-rh-negative.title: Anti-D if you're Rh (D) negative
anti-d-if-rh-negative.detail: If your blood group is Rh (D) negative, you may be offered anti-D injections, often around 28 weeks.

rsv-vaccine.title: Ask about the RSV vaccine
rsv-vaccine.detail: Offered from 28 weeks in the UK, or at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season in the US. It helps protect your baby in their first months.

sleep-on-side.title: Go to sleep on your side
sleep-on-side.detail: From 28 weeks, side-sleeping is safest for your baby, including naps. If you wake on your back, just turn onto your side.

safe-sleep-space.title: Prepare a safe sleep space
safe-sleep-space.detail: A cot or Moses basket with a firm, flat, well-fitting mattress, and no pillows, bumpers or duvets.

feeding-plan.title: Think about feeding your baby
feeding-plan.detail: Learn about breastfeeding, bottle feeding or both, and where to find support in the first days.

write-birth-plan.title: Write your birth plan
write-birth-plan.detail: Note your preferences for pain relief, birth partners and the first hours after birth, and share it with your midwife or doctor.

save-key-contacts.title: Save key numbers and plan your journey
save-key-contacts.detail: Keep your maternity unit, birth partner and transport details in your phone and on paper. It isn't safe to drive yourself in labour.

install-car-seat.title: Install the car seat
install-car-seat.detail: Choose a rear-facing seat that suits your baby's weight, fit it in advance and practise taking it in and out.

pack-hospital-bag.title: Pack your hospital bag
pack-hospital-bag.detail: Include your notes, comfy clothes, nightwear, maternity pads, snacks, a phone charger, baby clothes and nappies.

group-b-strep.title: Ask about group B strep
group-b-strep.detail: In the US, testing is usually done between 36 and 38 weeks; in the UK it isn't routine. Ask what applies to you.

learn-labour-signs.title: Learn the signs of labour
learn-labour-signs.detail: Regular contractions, a show, backache or your waters breaking. Know when your maternity unit wants you to call.

postnatal-support-plan.title: Plan support for after the birth
postnatal-support-plan.detail: Think about meals, help at home and who you can call. Learn the signs of postnatal depression, which can affect anyone.

past-due-date-options.title: Discuss going past your due date
past-due-date-options.detail: Ask about membrane sweeps, induction and extra monitoring, so you know your options before 41 weeks.
